title: Memory Reconsolidation
subtitle: Updating a reactivated memory under specific conditions
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating memory reconsolidation across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain memory reconsolidation in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in memory reconsolidation.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to memory reconsolidation.

sections.explainSimply: When a memory is reactivated, it may become temporarily modifiable before restabilising.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Clinical change may involve new learning and altered emotional meaning, but not every retrieval event opens a reconsolidation window.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Prediction error, retrieval conditions and timing matter in laboratory paradigms; translation to psychotherapy is promising but mechanistically uncertain.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of memory reconsolidation as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need memory reconsolidation to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not label all successful therapy “reconsolidation.”
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use memory reconsolidation to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses memory reconsolidation to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not label all successful therapy “reconsolidation.” Evidence classification: promising mechanism; clinical uncertainty.
